title: Is game dev now your new "game"? How many are doing it just for fun?
author: HereToLearn321
selftext:
I imagine many are trying to cash in on the "gold rush" . But how  many of you little \_\_\_ are doing it just for the pure fun of making quick little games (or  even large games)?



Anyone just making prototype after prototype and not even putting it online anywhere? Just want to see your little ideas come alive?

I always wanted to make a game and make my own models. I’ve started using blender to make a model and I’m really enjoying it. It’s so much fun!!

comments.author: Muito-Fish123
comments.body:
This is kind of my mentality, I have been working on a concept for 9 months now that merges features from Stellaris and HOI4. Sure I could go and play those games, but there is always a feature or mechanic that you don't really enjoy, so I am taking inspiration and developing those features that I would like to see for my own game. 

About the "gold rush" I think that is just survivorship bias, you only ever hear about successes so it makes game dev seem easy but I would say it's a lonely and hard path, you can pour your heart out for months / years and get nothing in return.

comments.author: Gigaslavx
comments.body: The rush is real. It's an oversaturated market now with low barries to entry. Don't expect to make money as a beginner. If anything standards and expectations have risen, and people can spot AI slop more easy. Don't expect to easily find a job either after learning for a bit. If anything game dev jobs were already underpaid before AI. I'd say you need to be medium level at least with general programming experience and education to make any money of it

replies.author: OldSlash
replies.body:
I work in mobile game dev, and I'd say the work is pretty different from making your own games. I have pet projects too, but at my current job I mostly deal with legal compliance, SDK updates, optimization, purchase validation, security issues, and all that stuff.

Actually, over the last four years at my current company, I've probably spent only about 5% of my time working on gameplay. The rest has been meta systems, compliance, optimization, bug fixes, etc.

And I think beginners will have a hard time dealing with all of this in their own projects, even though AI has made it much easier to get started.

replies.author: toni_btrain
replies.body: Can’t Claude do all that stuff?

replies.author: OldSlash
replies.body: It can, and it does, but there are some nuances. You still need technical expertise to understand what you're doing, define proper acceptance criteria, and evaluate the results. Even with the right settings, AI often makes decisions that are not optimal or produces code that passes all tests and looks good but would never work in a high-load live-ops production environment.

I've had a few goes at different games, now I'm at a point where I want to build and release a simpler game (that's not a full RTS game) which is built on the engine I've created - but this tangent game is leveraging AI to deliver on top of the engines capabilities I've built.

The way I look at it is if I can get a mildly successful game out that people enjoy and buy them that can fund experts that specialise in the things I'm missing e.g. modelling and animation, CGI etc, then my dream RTS can be built and realised for it's full potential.

Again progress with AI let's me make what I can't without it.

comments.author: NeusomaDev
comments.body:
I basically started my main project because I got fed up with Helldivers 2 lol.

My friends and I play PvE co-op squad shooters regularly, and we've found a few games over the years that lasted us a while. Usually, when we get tired of a game after playing it a while, it's a happy ending: we got way more hours out of it than a dev team reasonably could expect, of course it went stale over time, that's expected and fine, thanks for the memories. HD2 is the only game we played that we fell in love with, and that actively pushed us away before it went stale naturally. I was actually going to jump in on the HD2 vibe modding scene, but it was correctly pointed out to me that I should make my own game with my original ideas instead. Spending creative effort saving someone else's idea is risky business and limits your own ceiling: you're stuck with their foundation, good and bad, and especially in a live service game like that one, you're risking your whole project getting nuked on a whim.

TBH I think I would've bailed on this before now if a suitably good PvE co-op squad shooter hooked me. But none did - we've got decent ones in the rotation but none that have me obsessively interested - and at this point it's more fun to work on mine instead.

comments.author: heytumbleweed
comments.body:
I'm working full-time as a senior software developer, and gaming has been a huge part of my life for as long as I can remember. I follow new releases, keep up with the indie scene, and generally spend way too much time thinking about games, even when I'm not playing them.

With how quickly AI has been improving lately, I've started making my own little games and prototypes. And honestly, it's been a lot of fun.

The problem is that I keep getting stuck in the same loop. I get an idea, build a quick prototype, like how it turns out, and start expanding it into something bigger. Then, as the scope grows, another idea pops into my head and suddenly I'm more interested in building that instead.

The funny thing is, I had exactly the same problem before AI. Even when I was writing everything manually, I'd start building a website or an app, get excited about it, and eventually lose interest once the project became too big. AI hasn't created this problem for me, but it's definitely made it worse.

And there's another side to it. It feels like everyone is making games now. You come up with an idea you think is original, get excited, start building it, and halfway through you discover someone else has already made or announced something very similar.

So you move on to the next idea. And then it happens again.

Of course, this was happening before AI too. But back then, development took longer and the barrier to entry was higher. Now everything moves so fast that I sometimes feel this constant pressure to finish and release something before someone else does.

It's exhausting, honestly.

And to answer your original question, I think there's another part of this that comes with being an adult and working in software.

You start making something purely because you enjoy it. But at some point, you realize it could potentially make money. And once that thought gets into your head, it's hard to completely ignore it. You start thinking about your family, responsibilities, bills, and whether this little hobby could eventually become another source of income.

Before you know it, something that started as a fun creative project slowly turns into another thing you feel like you need to make successful.

I still genuinely enjoy making games. I just wish it were easier to keep that feeling separate from all the pressure around it.
